SynCLIP: Synonym-Coherent Language-Image.narr: CLIP-based detectors and segmenters fail when the language shifts—'coffee mug' and 'ceramic mug' should point to the same object, but produce completely different spatial attention maps. Semantic-consistent spatial attention alignment explicitly synchronizes the attention patterns across synonyms during pretraining, so the visual features respond consistently to any words that mean the same thing. This prevents inconsistency in dense predictions across linguistic variation.
SynCLIP: Synonym-Coherent Language-Image.how:
The problem: during contrastive training, each image-text pair pulls its match together, but synonyms like 'coffee mug' and 'ceramic mug' train independently, so they can learn completely different spatial attention patterns—a pixel may light up strongly for one synonym but not the other.

The mechanism: during pretraining, for each batch sample, the model identifies all known synonyms of its text caption using a language resource. When computing the contrastive loss, it treats all synonyms of the image's caption as matching pairs, pulling their embeddings toward the same image embedding simultaneously. This forces the encoder to route spatial attention consistently across semantically identical terms.

Why it works: by coercing synonyms to produce similar spatial features during training, downstream dense tasks (detection, segmentation) receive consistent signal regardless of which synonym the user types at test time.

Looking Beyond the Window: Global-Local.narr: High-resolution segmentation with CLIP requires sliding-window inference, but processing each window independently breaks semantic continuity—objects at window boundaries get mislabeled because each window sees only its local context. Global-local attention normalization dynamically rescales attention across windows using globally representative proxy queries, so a pixel near the edge sees its full semantic context, not just what fits in one window. The result: consistent pixel labels across the entire image, not a patchwork.
Looking Beyond the Window: Global-Local.how:
The problem: high-resolution segmentation runs CLIP in sliding windows (each 336×336 pixels), but each window is scored independently against text. A pixel near a window boundary sees only its local context, missing global semantic information that determines whether it matches the query.

The mechanism: construct a set of 'proxy queries'—global representative feature samples drawn from the full image—and during each window's attention computation, normalize each attention head using these global proxies as a reference. Specifically, for each position in a window, reweight its attention scores using statistics computed over the full image's proxy features, so local patches see themselves in global context.

Why it works: re-anchoring window-local attention scores to global statistics prevents the arbitrary boundary effects that occur when each window independently maximizes its own local similarity, yielding semantically coherent labels across the entire image.

Do Visual-Language Grid Maps Capture Lat.narr: A robot builds a semantic map by embedding images with CLIP and storing the features at each location—but does this map actually generalize to new scenes and queries? Without a rigorous evaluation methodology, teams deploy maps blind to their actual semantic quality. This paper defines semantic coverage metrics and transfer benchmarks that measure whether the embedding space truly captures object identity across viewpoints and instances.
Do Visual-Language Grid Maps Capture Lat.how:
The problem: robots build semantic maps by storing CLIP embeddings at each location in a grid. But without rigorous evaluation, these maps remain black boxes—does the embedding space actually capture object identity across different viewpoints, lighting, and instances of the same category?

The mechanism: create benchmarks that measure (1) semantic coverage: given a query embedding for 'table', can the map recover all table instances visible in that scene? (2) transfer: embed the same object from two different camera angles and measure whether their embeddings stay close enough to recognize it as the same thing. (3) cross-scene generalization: can a map built in Scene A recognize query concepts when applied to Scene B?

Why it works: by systematically measuring whether embeddings remain coherent across viewpoint, instance, and scene variations, the paper identifies which map regions are genuinely useful for a robot's navigation and which are brittle to distribution shift—guiding which embeddings to trust.

Learning Generalizable Feature Fields fo.narr: Mobile manipulation needs a single scene representation that handles both fine-grained geometry (where exactly do I grasp?) and large-scale spatial structure (how do I navigate there?). Unified feature fields that couple visual embeddings with geometric detail let the robot query the space by language for both high-level navigation targets and low-level grasp affordances, replacing the traditional separation between semantic maps and geometric models.
Learning Generalizable Feature Fields fo.how:
The problem: mobile manipulation requires two different scene representations: fine geometric detail for grasping (millimeter precision on where to contact), and large-scale spatial structure for navigation (meter-scale distances and reachability). Traditionally, teams use separate models (SLAM geometry + CLIP semantics), forcing robots to query two unrelated spaces.

The mechanism: distill CLIP embeddings directly into a continuous 3D feature field (represented as a NeRF or similar implicit function). At any 3D location (x, y, z), query the field to retrieve a language-aligned feature. Train the field so that positions with the same semantic meaning (e.g., all positions on the 'handle') cluster in embedding space, while preserving spatial locality—nearby points in 3D are nearby in feature space.

Why it works: a single unified field couples visual semantics with spatial proximity, so a robot can query 'navigate to a counter' to get a navigation waypoint, then zoom in and query 'grasp the handle' to get a precise contact point, both from the same continuous representation.

SRA-Det: Omni-Grained Open-Vocabulary De.narr: Open-vocabulary detectors score boxes against category embeddings, but real queries are richer: 'red mug' is not just 'mug'—it combines identity and color, and simple text embedding misses that faceted structure. Semantic Retrieval Augmentation with learnable semantic facets decomposes queries into multiple fine-grained attributes and reasons over them jointly, scoring boxes by soft-min matching that weighs all facets. The detector now sees 'red' as a separate semantic signal, not noise mixed into the 'mug' embedding.
SRA-Det: Omni-Grained Open-Vocabulary De.how:
The problem: open-vocabulary detectors score each region box against text embeddings for class names like 'mug' or 'chair'. But real queries are compositional: 'red mug' is not simply 'mug' + noise. A detector that embeds 'red mug' as a single embedding misses the structure—the redness and mugness are separate signals that interact.

The mechanism: within the region feature representation, learn to decompose into multiple semantic facets (category, color, shape, parts) by factorizing the region's vector space. At training time, annotate rich queries with their facet labels. At test time, for a query like 'red mug', encode 'red' and 'mug' separately into different embedding spaces, then score each region by soft-min matching—computing affinity scores for each facet independently and combining them via a learned soft-minimum operation that handles conflicting signals gracefully.

Why it works: by treating 'red' and 'mug' as independent signals rather than a monolithic embedding, the detector learns that redness is optional and can fail independently from category; soft-min aggregation ensures a region scores high only if it aligns on the facets that actually matter.

PET-DINO: Unifying Visual Cues into Grou.narr: Grounding DINO detects and grounds objects using visual prompts (a reference image or box), but prompt diversity—different image angles, lighting, backgrounds—hurts generalization. Training-time visual prompt augmentation is expensive and often suboptimal. Prompt-enriched training with dynamic memory distillation learns to transform diverse visual prompts into stable features that align with text embeddings, so the detector generalizes across prompt variations without manual augmentation.
PET-DINO: Unifying Visual Cues into Grou.how:
The problem: Grounding DINO detects objects using visual prompts (a reference image or bounding box of a similar object), but visual prompts vary in angle, lighting, and background. Naive prompt encoding fails when test-time prompts differ sharply from training examples.

The mechanism: during training, apply strong image augmentations to visual prompts (rotate, blur, change background) and use memory-augmented distillation: maintain a learnable memory bank of prompt embeddings and update it with moving averages of the detector's feature outputs as it processes diverse prompts. When a new prompt arrives at test time, retrieve similar prompts from memory and use them to refine the new prompt's embedding through attention over memory. This transforms arbitrary prompt variations into stable features aligned with the text embedding space.

Why it works: by learning stable prompt representations during training and anchoring test-time prompts to learned memory patterns, the detector generalizes to prompt variations it never directly trained on.

ViTPrompt: Training-Free Prompt Refineme.narr: Test-time refinement for open-vocabulary detection usually improves classification confidence but leaves bounding boxes noisy, since boxes and classes are optimized separately. Inserting visual tokens from high-confidence detections directly into the text prompt adds instance-aware geometric context without any retraining. Visual token augmentation lets the prompt encoder see the spatial structure the detector already found, refining both box coordinates and scores in a single pass.
ViTPrompt: Training-Free Prompt Refineme.how:
The problem: at test time, refining open-vocabulary detections to get sharper boxes typically requires choosing between two bad options: use the text prompt alone (class names are accurate but spatial reasoning is blurry) or iteratively optimize boxes (slow and often diverges).

The mechanism: take the detector's highest-confidence region (which the detector has already placed accurately) and extract visual tokens from that region using the ViT encoder. Insert these visual tokens directly into the text prompt encoder alongside the class name tokens. The text encoder now sees 'mug' tokens plus spatial context from the already-accurate box region, and can refine both the classification confidence and box coordinates in a single pass, without any backward passes through weights.

Why it works: because the detector already placed the box reasonably, adding visual context from it to the prompt encoder lets the encoder refine coordinates and scores in-context, drawing on spatial information the text prompt lacks, all while keeping the detector frozen.

Detect Everything with Few Examples.narr: Open-world robot manipulation needs to detect object categories with only a handful of demonstrations, no fine-tuning, and low latency on the robot. Using ViT features extracted from few exemplars and prototype-based matching, the system learns an open-set detector on the fly. Few-shot prototypical detection with frozen ViT backbones trades off-line training time for real-time adaptation: exemplars seed prototypes, new images are scored by similarity to those prototypes, and the model generalizes across viewpoints and instances without touching the weights.
Detect Everything with Few Examples.how:
The problem: on a robot deployed to a new environment, the detection model hasn't seen categories specific to that place (e.g., 'coffee maker' in this specific kitchen). Training from scratch on a handful of examples is too slow; fine-tuning is computationally expensive.

The mechanism: use a frozen ViT backbone (already trained on general images) to extract features from both the few exemplar images and test images. For each exemplar category, compute a prototype—the mean feature across all exemplars of that category. At test time, for each region in a new image, compute its ViT feature and measure cosine similarity to each category prototype. Use the prototype with highest similarity as the predicted class, and use the similarity score as confidence. No gradient updates; pure inference.

Why it works: ViT features generalize across viewpoint and lighting because they're trained on diverse data. Prototypical matching relies only on feature similarity, not learned classifier weights, so the system adapts to new classes instantly using their exemplars without re-training.

Mitigating Objectness Bias for Open-Voca.narr: Open-vocabulary panoptic segmentation merges semantic and instance masks, but objectness heads trained on seen classes suppress masks of unseen objects by default—they're never seen as 'objects.' CLIP's text score tells you the semantic signal is there, but the objectness gate kills it. CLIP-conditioned objectness recalibration overrides the objectness head using CLIP scores as a gate signal: if CLIP is confident, the region is treated as foreground even if objectness disagrees.
Mitigating Objectness Bias for Open-Voca.how:
The problem: panoptic segmentation merges semantic and instance masks. Standard detectors include an 'objectness' head trained on seen classes to distinguish foreground objects from background. When an unseen class appears (e.g., 'fork' if the training set had no forks), the objectness head confidently predicts 'background' regardless, killing the semantic mask even when CLIP scores it highly.

The mechanism: override the objectness gate using CLIP's text scores as a confidence signal. For each candidate region, if CLIP's highest semantic score (e.g., cosine with 'fork' embedding) exceeds a threshold, treat the region as foreground regardless of the objectness head's opinion. The objectness head still serves its purpose for seen classes, but CLIP's score 'rescues' unseen categories by providing an independent signal that says 'this region might be a valid object.'

Why it works: objectness is learned from seen data, so it cannot know unseen classes exist. By gating on CLIP's semantic signal, the system trusts what it learns from large-scale image-text pretraining over what it learned from limited training labels.

PCA-Seg: Revisiting Cost Aggregation for.narr: Vision transformers compute cost aggregation—matching features between regions—but aggregation that works for closed-vocabulary segmentation often fails at fine-grained segmentation and unseen classes because it assumes known object geometry. Cost aggregation revisited for open-vocabulary dense prediction decouples feature matching from class-specific spatial priors, letting the model find object boundaries using pure feature consistency. Better aggregation works equally well for parts (within-object structure) and unseen categories, unifying the problem.
PCA-Seg: Revisiting Cost Aggregation for.how:
The problem: dense prediction matches every pixel's feature to text embeddings. But pixel-by-pixel matching is noisy: a stray pixel might match 'handle' due to texture coincidence. Closed-vocabulary systems regularize this with learned class-specific spatial priors, but open-vocabulary has no such priors.

The mechanism: aggregate matching costs over local neighborhoods before thresholding. For each pixel, compute cosine similarity to the text embedding for all pixels in a small window (e.g., 5×5). Smooth the resulting cost map using guided filtering or bilateral filtering that respects visual boundaries (color/texture edges remain sharp). Only after aggregation, threshold to produce binary masks. Parts and unseen categories now respect visual discontinuities, not cost-function noise.

Why it works: cost aggregation enforces that connected regions of similar appearance should share a label, a prior universal to all open-vocabulary tasks and image-driven (boundaries follow actual visual edges).

Reconstructing CLIP for Open-Vocabulary.narr: CLIP is trained on image-level classification, so its features are global and coarse—a 14×14 grid of patches. Dense prediction needs fine spatial detail that CLIP's pretraining didn't directly optimize. Multi-scale feature reconstruction with spatial pyramid pooling augments CLIP with dense intermediate representations and learnable spatial queries, recovering fine detail at multiple scales. The reconstructed model keeps CLIP's vocabulary while gaining the spatial precision dense tasks demand.
Reconstructing CLIP for Open-Vocabulary.how:
The problem: CLIP's features are global—trained on whole-image classification, so a single patch encodes information from the entire image. Dense prediction needs fine spatial resolution, but CLIP outputs only a 14×14 grid of patches where each patch has seen the whole picture, destroying the local detail that segmentation requires.

The mechanism: extract intermediate hidden layers from CLIP at multiple depths (not just the final output), where earlier layers retain finer spatial structure. Combine these multi-scale features via learned projection heads and spatial upsampling, recovering 4–5× denser feature grids than CLIP's final output. Train a lightweight decoder on top to predict per-pixel labels, distilling CLIP's semantic alignment onto high-resolution features.

Why it works: multi-scale intermediate features encode both coarse semantics (from late layers) and fine spatial detail (from early layers). Reconstructing CLIP's alignment at higher resolution preserves the vocabulary while gaining the spatial precision dense tasks demand.

Rethinking MLLM Itself as a Segmenter wi.narr: Multimodal LLMs have vision and language understanding built in, but segmentation typically requires bolting on specialist mask decoders on top, adding complexity, weight, and latency. What if you just extracted high-resolution visual features directly from the MLLM without a separate decoder? Direct high-resolution feature extraction from MLLM internals yields dense spatial features that can be projected to masks with a simple linear layer, making segmentation cheaper and keeping the MLLM frozen.
Rethinking MLLM Itself as a Segmenter wi.how:
The problem: multimodal LLMs understand both vision and language, but generating segmentation masks requires adding specialist decoder networks on top—extra weight, latency, and complexity that slow the model down.

The mechanism: extract intermediate feature maps directly from the MLLM's vision backbone (e.g., layer 24 of the visual encoder) without passing through language-generation layers. Reshape these features to spatial coordinates and project them to high resolution via bilinear upsampling. A single learned linear layer transforms these dense features to binary masks for a single query token, eliminating the need for a separate mask decoder.

Why it works: MLLM vision encoders already learn rich spatial-semantic features; the language layers are unnecessary for segmentation. Bypassing them and operating on the intermediate feature grid directly yields fast, frozen-MLLM segmentation without extra decoder overhead.

PEARL: Geometry Aligns Semantics for Tra.narr: Training-free segmentation with frozen VLMs relies on matching image features to text embeddings, but the VLM's global bias—it's trained for classification—fights the per-pixel precision you need. Procrustes alignment rotates the feature space to maximize separability between the target class and background, then Laplacian propagation smooths the resulting confidence map using spatial structure. No training needed; just geometric rotation and diffusion that push the frozen features toward sharper, more coherent boundaries.
PEARL: Geometry Aligns Semantics for Tra.how: Procrustes alignment rotates the frozen feature space to maximize the separability between target class and background along a single axis. The output is two distributions: pixels that correlate with the text embedding (positive) and pixels that don't (negative). Once separated, Laplacian smoothing propagates confidence scores across space using spatial neighbors, exploiting the fact that nearby pixels usually share the same label. No training loop; just linear algebra and diffusion.

The Power of Prior: Training-Free Segmen.narr: LLaVA understands language and vision but wasn't trained to segment, so feeding its features directly to text matching yields poor masks. Yet LLaVA does have semantic and spatial priors baked into its layers. Extracting features from the right layer and applying frozen cosine matching between dense visual features and text embeddings yields surprisingly strong segmentation without any additional training. The 'prior' is simply the feature quality LLaVA already learned.
The Power of Prior: Training-Free Segmen.how: LLaVA's intermediate layer features already contain spatial structure and semantic understanding from its pretraining—the 'prior.' Extract the feature grid (e.g., layer 24 output), reshape it to spatial coordinates, then compute cosine similarity between every position's feature and the query text embedding. This produces a heatmap. The network's learned prior does all the work; matching is just a dot product. No gradient updates needed.

Direct Segmentation without Logits Optim.narr: Traditional open-vocabulary segmentation iteratively optimizes logits—a slow, indirect loop. The paper reframes the problem as solving distribution discrepancy analytically: homogeneous regions (same semantics everywhere in the region) should map to the same text embedding, so formulate segmentation as a distribution-matching problem with a closed-form solution. No iteration, no optimization loops—just a direct matrix solve that runs in milliseconds and achieves competitive accuracy.
Direct Segmentation without Logits Optim.how: Segmentation as a distribution-discrepancy minimization problem: within a coherent region, every pixel should align to the same text embedding. Formulate this as finding an assignment of pixels to semantic labels that minimizes the variance of embeddings within each region—a well-known problem in linear algebra with a closed-form solution via matrix operations. Solve once, no iteration, in milliseconds.

SPAR: Single-Pass Any-Resolution ViT for.narr: Vision Transformers are pretrained at a fixed resolution, and dense prediction at higher resolutions requires sliding-window inference (slow) or extrapolation (unstable). Teacher-student distillation transfers spatial reasoning from a finely-strided sliding-window teacher to a single-pass student, so the student learns to produce high-resolution segmentation maps in one forward pass without the teacher's computational cost. The student inherits the teacher's spatial sensitivity while running 10-50× faster.
SPAR: Single-Pass Any-Resolution ViT for.how: A sliding-window teacher network processes high-resolution images carefully, learning what fine spatial detail looks like at each scale. A student network trained to mimic the teacher's outputs on low-resolution input learns to 'hallucinate' fine-grained spatial reasoning from coarse feature maps. At test time, the student skips the expensive sliding windows and runs once, inheriting the teacher's spatial sensitivity without the cost.

Towards Open-World Grasping with Large V.narr: Language-instructed grasping requires both semantic understanding ('grasp the red mug') and precise spatial-geometric reasoning (contact normals, collision checks). VLMs are strong at semantics but weak at spatial details; geometric models miss the language grounding. VLM referring segmentation combined with contact-aware grasp ranking uses the VLM to ground the referred object, then scores candidate grasp poses by contact point quality and clearance. Two streams—semantic and geometric—fuse into a single action.
Towards Open-World Grasping with Large V.how: A VLM grounds the referred object using semantic understanding, producing a segmentation mask of the target. Meanwhile, a separate geometric module scores candidate grasp poses based on contact point quality (pressure distribution, friction) and clearance (collision-free reaching). These two streams—semantic identification and geometric feasibility—combine via rank fusion or learned weighting to select the final grasp pose.

VLM-Grounder: A VLM Agent for Zero-Shot.narr: 3D visual grounding (pointing to an object in a point cloud based on language) usually needs 3D training data and 3D-aware architectures. Yet a 2D vision-language model can reason about spatial relations if given multiple views of the scene. Reasoning-chain distillation over multiview 2D VLM outputs projects 3D points to several viewpoints, scores each using the 2D VLM, and aggregates using learned spatial reasoning. Zero-shot 3D grounding reaches competitive accuracy on ScanRefer without 3D labels or 3D-specific training.
VLM-Grounder: A VLM Agent for Zero-Shot.how: Project 3D points into multiple 2D viewpoints (e.g., 5 camera angles). Embed each viewpoint with the 2D VLM and score regions using the text query. Aggregate scores over viewpoints using learned spatial reasoning—effectively asking the VLM to vote from multiple angles—then select the 3D region with the highest consensus. Zero-shot because the 2D VLM has never seen 3D coordinates, yet multiview aggregation recovers 3D spatial understanding.

DeRVOS: Decoupling Trajectory Generation.narr: Referring video segmentation must track a specific referred object ('the person in the red coat') across occlusions and motion in dynamic scenes. Unified models that jointly handle temporal tracking and multimodal fusion often fail under occlusion. Decoupling into consistent trajectory generation and multimodal understanding uses a pretrained video instance segmentation model to generate candidate trajectories, then multimodal fusion selects which trajectory matches the referring expression. Separation of concerns simplifies the problem.
DeRVOS: Decoupling Trajectory Generation.how: A pretrained video instance segmentation model (trained on class-agnostic motion) generates candidate object trajectories across frames, each with temporal consistency. A multimodal fusion module (VLM + video features) then selects which trajectory matches the referring expression by comparing the trajectory's appearance and motion to the text query. Separation of concerns: temporal tracking is solved by a generalist, language grounding by a specialist.

ThinkGrasp: A Vision-Language System for.narr: Grasping heavily occluded objects in clutter requires reasoning about what's hiding beneath and whether removing obstacles first makes sense—pure visual geometry can't answer 'should I move the thing on top of it first?' A vision-language system that reasons about occlusion relationships and strategic removal jointly considers the visible geometry, the language description of the target, and the spatial graph of what's blocking what. The system plans not just where to grasp, but whether the grasp order matters.
ThinkGrasp: A Vision-Language System for.how: From a single image, a VLM reasons about the spatial graph of what's occluding what (e.g., 'the book is on top of the mug'). The system then plans a grasp sequence: if the target is occluded, remove the obstacle first, then grasp the target. The VLM encodes task intent and occlusion reasoning; a motion planner converts the reasoned strategy into executable grasp poses. The language reasoning bridges the perceptual gap that geometry alone cannot cross.

GraspSAM: When Segment Anything Meets Gr.narr: Grasp detection usually fails on unfamiliar objects because training data is limited, and users can't easily direct the system to specific regions. GraspSAM adapts SAM (trained on 1B masks) with lightweight adapters and a modified decoder, accepting point, box, or text prompts to predict grasps for any object without category labels. By reusing SAM's massive prior knowledge, the system generalizes to unseen object types and multiple prompt modalities.
GraspSAM: When Segment Anything Meets Gr.how: SAM is trained on 1 billion masks—a massive prior for any segmentation task. Fine-tune SAM's decoder and add lightweight adapters (low-rank modules) on the encoder to specialize for grasps, while keeping the backbone frozen. Accept text prompts (or points, boxes) and output grasp-specific masks. The massive pre-trained prior from CLIP and SAM transfers directly; only a small adapter layer learns grasp geometry from labeled examples.

SAM-Rectified Part Detection with Iterat.narr: Parts like handles, wheels, and buttons have different geometric and functional properties that affect how a robot should interact with them, yet SAM segments them as visual regions without understanding their distinct roles. The gap is that part segmentation needs to recognize functional identity, not just visual boundaries. This approach fine-tunes SAM on parts, then iteratively refines part masks by matching pose predictions: it detects a part's orientation and pose from the mask, re-prompts SAM with refined regions, and repeats to converge on part masks that align to actual functional geometry.
SAM-Rectified Part Detection with Iterat.how: SAM is prompted with a region hypothesis. The model outputs a mask. Fit the mask to a geometric model (e.g., a cylinder for a handle) and predict the part's pose (orientation, position) from the mask shape and image features. Re-prompt SAM with the predicted pose geometry as a refined bounding box or constraint. Iterate: mask → pose → refined prompt → better mask. Convergence happens in 2–3 rounds, each refining the functional geometry.

MovSAM: Single-Image Moving Object Segme.narr: Detecting moving objects normally requires comparing multiple frames—impossible from a single still image. An MLLM reasons step-by-step about scene context to infer motion cues, generating text prompts that SAM uses to segment likely-moving objects with iterative refinement. Semantic reasoning about object behavior bridges the temporal gap that optical flow cannot cross from one image alone.
MovSAM: Single-Image Moving Object Segme.how: An MLLM (multimodal LLM) reasons step-by-step about what likely moved in the scene based on context: 'the person is standing still, so things they touch might be moving.' The LLM generates a descriptive text prompt (e.g., 'objects being held or manipulated'). SAM then segments regions matching that semantic description. Iterative refinement: the MLLM scores candidate masks, refines the prompt, and SAM re-segments. Language reasoning compensates for the missing temporal signal.

Low-Effort Iterative Dataset Generation.narr: Hand-labeling instance masks for unfamiliar objects is expensive and limits training data diversity. Change detection (frame differencing) identifies unfamiliar objects automatically, then SAM auto-labels them without human annotation, bootstrapping datasets for new categories. Iterative refinement over multiple frames converges to accurate masks.
Low-Effort Iterative Dataset Generation.how: Frame differencing (subtracting consecutive frames) automatically identifies changing regions—likely unseen objects. SAM auto-labels these regions without human annotation. Over multiple frames, the system refines masks by re-prompting SAM and filtering for consistency. Aggregation across frames gives converged masks. The loop is: detect change → SAM labels → collect → refine → new dataset ready, all unsupervised.

Ov3R: Open-Vocabulary Semantic 3D Recons.narr: 3D scene understanding has always required category-specific labels, making it impossible to recognize objects outside the training vocabulary. CLIP3R fuses 2D CLIP embeddings with camera geometry to build instance-level open-vocabulary reconstruction, attaching language-aligned features to each voxel. A single video and a text prompt suffice to locate and segment any object in 3D without 3D training labels.
Ov3R: Open-Vocabulary Semantic 3D Recons.how: Structure-from-motion builds a sparse 3D point cloud and camera poses. For each 3D point, project it into every frame where it's visible and extract CLIP patch features from those pixels. Average the CLIP features across views to get a view-consistent language-aligned descriptor per point. Cluster points by feature similarity and assign text labels via CLIP scoring. No 3D labels needed; 2D language-aligned features lift directly to 3D via camera geometry.

CoSMo3D: Promptable 3D Semantic Segmenta.narr: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation must handle partial views and compositional phrases like 'the handle of the mug. ' An LLM guides construction of a canonical shape space where semantically similar parts align across views, then queries are matched in that stable space. Canonical alignment lets the system reason about part identity and spatial attributes without 3D training data.
CoSMo3D: Promptable 3D Semantic Segmenta.how: An LLM analyzes the query (e.g., 'the handle of the mug') and constructs a canonical shape prototype—an idealized 3D model of what a handle looks like. Observed 3D geometry is aligned to this canonical space, where semantically similar parts across instances overlap. Queries are matched in canonical space, where geometric variation is minimized. Canonical alignment lets compositional queries work zero-shot without 3D training data.

OpenVoxel: Training-Free Grouping and Ca.narr: Voxel grids provide a simple 3D representation, but they lack semantic labels and grouping — you have occupied voxels but no understanding of which voxels belong to the same object or what that object is. The challenge is achieving object-level semantic understanding in 3D without training on 3D labels. OpenVoxel groups voxels using unsupervised clustering, then uses a frozen MLLM to caption each cluster by reasoning about its geometry and appearance: it performs clustering on voxel positions and features, then queries an MLLM with the cluster's geometry and color to generate a natural-language description, enabling open-vocabulary queries without training.
OpenVoxel: Training-Free Grouping and Ca.how: Discretize the 3D space into a voxel grid. Use unsupervised clustering (e.g., connected-components analysis or density-based clustering) on voxel positions and color features to group occupied voxels into objects. For each cluster, query an MLLM with the cluster's geometry (point cloud), color distribution, and context to generate a natural-language caption. The MLLM reasons about the cluster's visual and spatial properties. No 3D training data; caption acts as the semantic label.

OpenVox: Real-Time Instance-Level Open-V.narr: Mobile robots need fast, incremental open-vocabulary 3D maps, but real-time segmentation noise accumulates across frames, corrupting the map. A probabilistic voxel SLAM fuses VLM-grounded instances across frames using per-voxel membership probabilities, smoothing detection errors through time. Instance tracking persists object identity even when individual frames are ambiguous.
OpenVox: Real-Time Instance-Level Open-V.how: A probabilistic voxel SLAM maintains per-voxel membership probabilities for detected object instances. When a new frame arrives with VLM-detected regions, update each voxel's probability of belonging to each instance using Bayesian fusion across frames. Noisy detections in one frame are smoothed by history; instance identity persists even when the current frame is ambiguous. Real-time incremental updates replace expensive batch reconstruction.

GraspSplats: Efficient Manipulation with.narr: Continuous 3D fields (NeRFs) encode language-aligned features but require expensive differentiable rendering to sample grasp poses; discrete voxels waste memory. Distilled CLIP features attach directly to 3D Gaussians, enabling direct grasp point sampling via feature lookup rather than rendering. This explicit geometry avoids neural field inference overhead while capturing scenes in 60 seconds.
GraspSplats: Efficient Manipulation with.how: 3D Gaussian splatting encodes 3D geometry with a compact set of Gaussians (splats). For each Gaussian, project it into visible frames and extract CLIP features from the projected pixels. Distill and attach the averaged CLIP feature directly to the Gaussian. At test time, query the scene by scoring splats against text embeddings; top-scored splats form the grasp target. No expensive NeRF inference; features live on geometry.

LensDFF: Language-Enhanced Sparse Featur.narr: Few-shot dexterous manipulation is computationally expensive when systems must reconstruct full 3D scenes (NeRF) for each new object from limited views. 2D visual features distill directly onto simple point clouds, with text descriptions guiding view-consistent feature fusion for single-view generalization. Avoiding full scene reconstruction cuts computational cost while enabling grasp generalization.
LensDFF: Language-Enhanced Sparse Featur.how: Project 2D CLIP features onto a sparse point cloud (e.g., 10k points from structure-from-motion). Text descriptions guide view-consistent fusion: features from multiple views of the same point are averaged using learned weights that favor consistent, high-confidence alignments. Distill dense 2D features onto sparse 3D points, retaining only language-aligned information. Sparse representation cuts memory while enabling single-view grasp generalization.

DVEFormer: Efficient Dense Visual Embedd.narr: Real-time open-vocabulary scene understanding requires per-pixel language-aligned features, but VLM inference is slow and desktop-bound. Knowledge distillation from an Alpha-CLIP teacher trains an efficient RGB-D Transformer student to predict dense embeddings at 26–77 FPS, running directly on edge hardware. The compact student inherits CLIP alignment without recomputing expensive VLM features.
DVEFormer: Efficient Dense Visual Embedd.how: An expensive Alpha-CLIP teacher processes RGB-D images and outputs per-pixel language-aligned features. A lightweight Transformer student (trained on sequences of RGB-D patches) learns to predict the teacher's dense embeddings from input frames in real time. Knowledge distillation transfers the teacher's alignment into a 26–77 FPS student that runs on edge hardware. Compact student inherits CLIP semantics without recomputing expensive VLM features.

ExtrinSplat: Decoupling Geometry and Sem.narr: 3D Gaussian splats were designed for geometry — reconstructing shape and appearance from images. Adding semantic features directly to splats conflates two separate problems: some splats might represent background geometry that has no semantic label, while others represent objects that are semantically important. ExtrinSplat decouples geometry splats (for accurate 3D shape) from semantic features (for language grounding): it maintains the original Gaussian geometry for rendering fidelity, but stores language-aligned features in a separate, task-specific layer, avoiding the contamination of geometry with semantic labels.
ExtrinSplat: Decoupling Geometry and Sem.how: 3D Gaussians originally encode both geometry (shape, appearance) and now semantic labels. This conflates two concerns: some splats might be background geometry with no semantic meaning, others are semantically significant foreground. Maintain two separate representations: geometry splats for rendering fidelity, semantic features in a separate language-aligned layer. Geometry is optimized for appearance reconstruction; semantics for language grounding. Decoupling prevents semantic noise from corrupting geometry and vice versa.

UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grou.narr: Grounding a phrase like 'the chair to the left of the desk' in a point cloud requires three capabilities: recognizing objects by open-vocabulary labels, understanding spatial relations (left, right, behind), and reasoning about geometry without 3D training data. The challenge is doing this zero-shot when the language grounding model has never seen 3D coordinates. UZ3DVG distills a reasoning-aware chain-of-thought from an MLLM into a geometry-aware 3D model: it uses an MLLM to generate a reasoning trace (identify candidates, check relations, select), then learns to reproduce that reasoning using 3D geometry features and spatial relations, achieving 3D grounding without 3D labels.
UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grou.how:
The problem: 3D visual grounding (locating 'the chair to the left of the desk' in a point cloud) requires understanding object identity (what is a chair?) and spatial relations (which chair is left of the desk?). Doing this zero-shot with a 2D vision-language model that has never seen 3D coordinates requires reasoning across modalities.

The mechanism: project 3D objects into multiple 2D viewpoints (e.g., 5–10 camera angles around the scene). Embed each viewpoint with a 2D VLM and score candidate objects using text-image similarity. Aggregate scores over viewpoints using learned spatial reasoning chains—ask the VLM to reason step-by-step about spatial relations ('which objects are chairs? which is to the left of the desk?') and distill that chain-of-thought reasoning into 3D geometry features. Multiview voting recovers 3D spatial understanding without 3D training data.

Why it works: 2D VLMs can reason about spatial relations through language; multiview projection recovers 3D understanding from 2D reasoning over multiple angles, and distillation compresses the reasoning into efficient geometry features.

SAQN: Semantic-Based Adaptive Query Netw.narr: 3D referring segmentation must resolve class identity and spatial relations simultaneously, but standard point-cloud networks treat them separately. Class-level semantic queries adapt per-instance to reconcile 'which object?' and 'which spatial role?' in a single pass over the point cloud. Adaptive routing lets the network focus on spatial reasoning necessary for disambiguation.
SAQN: Semantic-Based Adaptive Query Netw.how:
The problem: 3D referring segmentation must jointly resolve what an object is (class identity) and which specific role it plays (spatial relations, attributes). Standard networks treat these as separate problems, forcing the model to reason about identity and relations in tandem without specialization.

The mechanism: use class-level semantic embeddings to initialize learned query tokens at the start of the network. For each query token, adapt its parameters based on the semantic class scores computed over point-cloud features. Route features through an adaptive transformer where query-adaptation gates determine which spatial regions attend to which semantic signals. This coupling of semantic identity to spatial routing ensures that spatial reasoning is tuned to the specific class being grounded.

Why it works: adaptive routing lets the network focus computational resources on the spatial reasoning necessary for disambiguation; a mug-grounding query uses different spatial cues than a chair-grounding query, and adaptive routing specializes per-instance.

LangRef3DGS: Language-Guided 3D Referent.narr: Identifying 'the red mug in the cabinet' in a 3D Gaussian-splatted scene requires learning object identities from partial views that arrive incrementally. A Dirichlet process discovers latent object categories and maintains open-vocabulary identity across partial observations, grounding referring expressions without closed-set class labels. Non-parametric Bayesian inference lets the system add new identities as views arrive.
LangRef3DGS: Language-Guided 3D Referent.how:
The problem: 3D Gaussian splatting reconstructs geometry from multi-view RGB, but referring expressions require semantic understanding built from partial views that arrive incrementally. Without closed-set class labels, the system must learn object identities as observations accumulate.

The mechanism: use a Dirichlet process—a non-parametric Bayesian model—to maintain an open-ended set of latent object categories. As new frames arrive with partial views, update the process by (1) assigning each visible region to an existing category or creating a new one, (2) storing that assignment in the Gaussian splatting representation, (3) when grounding a phrase, match it against the discovered categories and their supporting splats. The DP automatically infers how many object identities exist as evidence accumulates.

Why it works: Dirichlet processes allow the system to discover new categories on-the-fly without predefined class limits, and Bayesian updates smoothly integrate new evidence across frames.

QueryMe: Open-Vocabulary 3D Object Affor.narr: A robot grasping an object must locate not just 'the mug' but 'the handle of the mug'—the interactive part. Multimodal reasoning over 3D evidence grounds affordances described in plain language, connecting task intent to geometric grasp opportunities. Task descriptions provide the semantic signal needed to resolve which part is actionable.
QueryMe: Open-Vocabulary 3D Object Affor.how:
The problem: grounding a task-relevant affordance like 'where do I insert the key?' requires reasoning about function, not just identity. A 3D object may have multiple interactable regions, and language describes which one matters for a specific task.

The mechanism: fuse multimodal evidence: (1) 2D image features from a VLM anchor the object in image space, (2) 3D point-cloud geometry provides shape understanding, (3) task description (e.g., 'insert key') guides which part is relevant. Score candidate 3D regions (point clusters) by combining VLM affordance reasoning ('where would a key insert?'), geometric fit (cavity detection, part alignment), and task context. Select the top-scored region as the affordance location.

Why it works: multimodal fusion balances semantic understanding (what task does this support?) with geometric evidence (does the shape allow it?), grounding affordances in both language and geometry.

Zoo3D: Zero-Shot 3D Object Detection at.narr: 3D object detection at scene level without training labels requires inferring object boundaries from geometry and appearance cues alone. SAM-generated masks cluster via graph structure to form connected 3D regions, with open-vocabulary classification applied to each cluster without any 3D detection training. Graph clustering enforces spatial coherence.
Zoo3D: Zero-Shot 3D Object Detection at.how:
The problem: 3D object detection usually requires training on labeled 3D bounding boxes, a heavy supervision requirement. Detecting objects without 3D training data requires inferring boundaries from geometry and appearance alone.

The mechanism: segment the RGB image into regions using SAM (Segment Anything Model), then build a graph where each segmented region becomes a node, and edges connect spatially adjacent regions. Use graph clustering (e.g., region-merging or community detection) to group similar regions into 3D objects, enforcing spatial coherence. For each cluster, classify it using open-vocabulary scoring (CLIP similarity to object names). Project clusters to 3D via camera geometry to recover bounding boxes.

Why it works: SAM provides zero-shot segmentation without class labels, graph clustering enforces spatial structure, and CLIP classification runs open-vocabulary scoring, combining all three to detect objects with no 3D training labels.

NoOVD: Novel Category Discovery for Open.narr: Open-vocabulary detection covers known classes but struggles to recognize genuinely new categories at deployment time. Metric learning discovers emerging clusters in feature space and assigns them embeddings compatible with the open-vocabulary model, expanding the detector's vocabulary without retraining. New categories integrate via embedding alignment.
NoOVD: Novel Category Discovery for Open.how:
The problem: open-vocabulary detectors cover known classes well, but genuinely new categories at deployment time are either forced onto the nearest known class (wrong) or flagged as unknown without learning them. The system never expands its vocabulary through deployment experience.

The mechanism: monitor detector outputs for emerging clusters in feature space that don't align well with any known-class embedding. Use metric learning to discover these clusters: compute distance distributions between region features and known-class embeddings, flag regions scoring low on all known classes as anomalies. Cluster these anomalies in feature space and assign them new embeddings aligned to the open-vocabulary model's space via learned projection. Add the new embeddings to the detector's vocabulary without retraining.

Why it works: metric learning detects regions that deviate from known patterns; assigning them aligned embeddings lets the detector incorporate new categories into the vocabulary immediately, expanding open-vocabulary grounding through deployment.

Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation for Robo.narr: Agricultural robots must recognize crops and distinguish weeds, but new weed species constantly emerge and crop varieties vary by region. The challenge is performing segmentation on unseen plant species and weed types without retraining. This approach models crop and weed classes as hyperspheres in a learned feature space, treating unfamiliar weeds as anomalies distant from known crop spheres: it learns a feature space where known crops form tight clusters (hyperspheres) and new weeds appear as outliers, enabling zero-shot detection of unseen species through anomaly scoring in feature space.
Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation for Robo.how:
The problem: agricultural robots must distinguish crops from weeds, but new weed species and crop varieties constantly emerge. Retraining for every new species is impractical; instead, the system must recognize crops as one semantic category and flag unfamiliar species as weeds.

The mechanism: learn a feature space where known crop classes form tight hyperspheres (clusters with small radius). For each crop species, compute the mean feature and radius of the training examples. At test time, score regions by distance to each crop hypersphere: a region close to a crop sphere is classified as that crop; a region far from all crop spheres is flagged as a weed (anomaly) via distance-from-known-centers scoring. Parts of weeds distant from any known crop sphere are marked as unknown.

Why it works: hypersphere clustering provides a geometric model of known classes; anomalies are regions outside all known spheres, enabling zero-shot detection of unseen weed species without retraining.

OoDIS: Anomaly Instance Segmentation and.narr: Autonomous vehicles encounter unknown objects at deployment, but benchmarks rarely measure instance-level segmentation and detection jointly. OoDIS extends anomaly segmentation benchmarks with instance-level tasks, standardizing evaluation across semantic and instance anomaly understanding. A unified benchmark reveals gaps between detecting unknowns and pinpointing each precisely.
OoDIS: Anomaly Instance Segmentation and.how:
The problem: autonomous vehicles encounter unknown objects at deployment, but most anomaly benchmarks evaluate only semantic segmentation (pixel-level unknowns) or detection (unknown bounding boxes). Instance-level grounding of unknowns—exactly which pixels/3D region constitute each anomaly object—is rarely measured, leaving gaps in evaluation.

The mechanism: create a benchmark dataset where scenes contain both known and unknown objects. For each unknown, provide pixel-level segmentation masks (semantic anomaly labels) and instance-level groupings (which pixels belong to which individual anomaly object), plus instance bounding boxes. Define evaluation metrics for both semantic and instance-level anomaly understanding: can the system detect unknowns AND separate multiple unknown objects from each other?

Why it works: a unified benchmark revealing the gap between detecting anomalies and pinpointing each one separately drives progress on the harder, more practical problem of instance-level anomaly understanding.

HOPS: Hierarchical Open-Vocabulary Part.narr: Object recognition stops at the category level — 'mug' — but manipulation requires finding specific parts within it. The challenge is that parts like handles, spouts, or buttons don't have a closed taxonomy; they're defined relationally within each object. HOPS tackles this by using hierarchical attention filtering: it extracts which spatial attention heads in a VLM strongly respond to a queried part description, then propagates those activations across the visual feature grid to form a part mask, all without pixel-level part labels.
HOPS: Hierarchical Open-Vocabulary Part.how:
The problem: object-level recognition ('mug') leaves out parts that matter for manipulation. Parts like handles, spouts, or buttons don't have a closed taxonomy; each object type defines them differently.

The mechanism: extract spatial attention maps from multiple heads in a VLM's transformer when processing a part query (e.g., 'handle of the mug'). Filter attention heads by comparing their outputs to a part text embedding—retain only heads that strongly activate on the handle. Propagate activations from the selected heads across the visual feature grid using affinity propagation (message passing that respects feature similarity) to build a dense part-level heatmap. Threshold and upsample to produce a part segmentation mask, all without pixel-level part labels.

Why it works: different attention heads specialize in different visual concepts; selecting heads that respond to a part query isolates the visual reasoning needed to find that part, and propagation ensures coherent boundaries.

PCA-Seg: Cost Aggregation for Semantic &.narr: Dense prediction of both objects and parts requires matching every pixel to semantic embeddings, but naive per-pixel matching is noisy and lacks spatial coherence. The problem is that pixels don't exist in isolation — a part boundary should align with actual visual discontinuities in texture or color. PCA-Seg solves this by aggregating similarity costs over local neighborhoods: rather than scoring each pixel independently against text embeddings, it smooths cost over neighborhoods before thresholding, recovering sharp boundaries aligned to visual edges while maintaining open-vocabulary generality.
PCA-Seg: Cost Aggregation for Semantic &.how:
The problem: dense prediction matches every pixel's feature to a text embedding. But pixel-by-pixel matching is noisy: a stray isolated pixel might match 'handle' due to texture coincidence, not true structure. Closed-vocabulary systems regularize this using learned class-specific spatial priors (smooth texture regions belong together), but open-vocabulary has no such priors.

The mechanism: aggregate matching costs over local neighborhoods before thresholding. For each pixel, instead of immediately comparing its feature to text, compute cosine similarity for all pixels in a small window (e.g., 5×5). Smooth this cost map using guided filtering or bilateral filtering that respects visual boundaries (color/texture edges remain sharp). Only after aggregation, threshold the smoothed cost to produce a binary mask. Parts or unseen categories now respect visual discontinuities in the image, not arbitrary cost function noise.

Why it works: cost aggregation enforces that connected regions of similar visual appearance should share a semantic label, a prior that's universal (works for parts, unseen classes, any dense prediction) and image-driven (boundaries follow actual visual edges).

SRA-Det: Detection Beyond Category Names.narr: Open-vocabulary detectors today score regions against category embeddings like 'mug' or 'chair', but real instructions often specify attributes ('red mug') or parts ('cup handle'). A single region vector is weak for decomposing these multi-faceted descriptions. SRA-Det breaks this by learning separate semantic facets within a detection backbone: it discovers sub-embeddings for category, color, texture, and parts within each region's features, then matches each facet independently to the query, enabling detection of 'red mug' without training on that exact phrase.
SRA-Det: Detection Beyond Category Names.how:
The problem: open-vocabulary detectors embed queries like 'red mug' as a single vector, but 'red' and 'mug' are independent attributes. A region may match 'mug' but not be red; forcing both into one embedding forces the detector to treat them as inseparable, losing expressiveness.

The mechanism: within the region feature space, learn to factorize semantic facets—category, color, shape, parts—by decomposing the region's representation into multiple sub-embeddings during training. At test time, for a query like 'red mug', encode 'red' into one facet embedding and 'mug' into another. Score each region by soft-min matching: compute affinity scores for each facet independently, then combine using a learnable soft-minimum operation that gracefully handles conflicting signals (a region can score high overall even if one facet is weak).

Why it works: soft-min aggregation ensures regions are scored high only when all salient facets match; treating facets independently prevents one failing attribute from drowning out matching ones.

Part-Aware Vision-Language Models for Fi.narr: Vision-language models align images to text at the whole-object level, but to recognize fine-grained distinctions — like different handle styles or mug shapes — they must align parts of the image to parts of the description. Without explicit part-level correspondence, a VLM can miss what makes objects different. This approach adds part alignment inside the VLM training: it grounds text mentions of parts ('the curved handle', 'the flat rim') directly to corresponding image regions during contrastive training, so the model learns part-level correspondences that boost fine-grained recognition.
Part-Aware Vision-Language Models for Fi.how:
The problem: standard vision-language models align images to text at the whole-object level—a photo of a mug aligns to 'mug.' But fine-grained distinctions (different handle styles, rim shapes) require aligning specific image regions to specific text phrases describing those parts.

The mechanism: during contrastive pretraining, include part-level annotations in captions (e.g., 'a mug with a curved handle' or 'the handle of the mug'). For each part mention in the text, extract the corresponding region from the image using bounding-box or segmentation supervision. Align part-region features to part-text embeddings directly during training, adding part-level contrastive losses alongside the whole-image alignment. This forces spatial attention to focus on the described parts.

Why it works: explicit part-level correspondence during training makes the model learn which visual regions correspond to which textual parts, improving fine-grained recognition by grounding language descriptions to the image structure they describe.

AffordGrasp: In-Context Affordance Reaso.narr: A robot that knows 'mug' doesn't automatically know where to grasp it — affordances (grasp points, push surfaces) depend on the task, not just the object type. When the task is 'pour', the handle is the grasp point; for 'clean', the body is better. The gap is that no label set can enumerate all task-object affordance pairs. AffordGrasp uses an MLLM to infer affordances from task instructions in context: it queries the model with the task description ('pour the coffee into the cup'), the VLM reasons about which part affords that action, then a part segmenter locates it, bridging from words and intent to actionable pose.
AffordGrasp: In-Context Affordance Reaso.how:
The problem: a robot recognizing 'mug' doesn't automatically know where to grasp it. Affordances depend on the task: pouring requires the handle, while cleaning prefers the body. No fixed label set covers all task-object pairs.

The mechanism: query a VLM with the task instruction in-context: 'given that you need to pour the coffee into the cup, which part of the mug should you grasp?' The VLM reasons about task semantics and infers the affordance (e.g., 'hold the handle and tilt'). Then ground the inferred part using an open-vocabulary part segmenter: localize 'handle' in the image. Finally, fit a 6-DOF grasp pose to the located handle region, using contact-point geometry and approach axis to define the grasp. The language reasoning bridges from task intent to actionable geometry.

Why it works: VLM reasoning grounds task intent to part identity; part segmentation grounds identity to pixels; grasp pose generation converts pixels to actionable poses. The chain preserves semantic intent through geometric execution.

RoboPoint: A VLM for Spatial Affordance.narr: Affordances are spatial — they're keypoints or contact regions where interaction succeeds. Naming objects is different from pinpointing where to act on them, yet most models conflate the two. The challenge is predicting action keypoints (grasp points, push locations, insertion ports) for objects never seen in training. RoboPoint frames affordance prediction as keypoint regression in image coordinates: given an object and a task description, it predicts the pixel coordinates where a robot should act, using VLM reasoning to ground task semantics to 2D action points, zero-shot across new objects.
RoboPoint: A VLM for Spatial Affordance.how: The VLM encodes the image and task description into a shared embedding space, then produces a regression head that outputs pixel (x, y) coordinates. The key operation is a spatial attention module over the image features that focuses on regions relevant to the task, amplifying features near where the task can be executed. The regression head treats affordance prediction as a heatmap generation problem: for each spatial location in the feature grid, it computes a confidence score by comparing that location's features against the task embedding, yielding a dense affordance map that peaks at actionable pixels.

MOKA: Open-World Manipulation through Ma.narr: Robots must reason about how to manipulate unfamiliar objects in open-world settings, but traditional approaches require category-specific policies or dense affordance labels. The problem is bridging from semantic understanding of an object to deciding where and how to grasp or manipulate it, without closed-form affordance labels. MOKA frames affordance reasoning as VLM question-answering over marked regions: it shows the VLM object regions with spatial markers and asks 'which region should I grasp to accomplish X?', letting the model reason through affordances as natural language rather than predicting coordinate outputs.
MOKA: Open-World Manipulation through Ma.how:
1. The system overlays spatial markers (colored boxes or dots) on segmented object regions in the input image.
  2. The marked image and task query ('grasp to open') are concatenated into a single prompt text, passed to the VLM.
  3. The VLM attends to both the marked regions and the task description in a unified sequence, outputting natural language ('the handle at the top-left region') that grounds the affordance explanation.
  4. Unlike coordinate regression, this taps the VLM's language generation to reason about spatial relationships directly, avoiding the bottleneck of quantized pixel coordinates.

SemSegGrasp: Task-Oriented Grasping via.narr: Grasping depends on the task: picking up a coffee cup requires grasping the handle, but if the cup is empty and upright, any region works. Most grasping pipelines ignore the semantic task and predict regions uniformly. The key insight is that semantic understanding of an object's parts and their properties should directly drive grasp point selection. SemSegGrasp combines open-vocabulary part segmentation with grasp pose generation: it segments task-relevant parts ('handle', 'body', 'rim') using open-vocab labels, then fits grasp poses to these semantically meaningful regions, ensuring grasps align with task requirements.
SemSegGrasp: Task-Oriented Grasping via.how: An open-vocabulary segmentation model (e.g., CLIP-driven) outputs per-pixel class labels for task-relevant parts ('handle', 'lid', 'drawer-knob'). Each predicted part region forms a 3D point cloud segment by unprojecting the 2D mask using depth. A grasp pose generator then samples candidate gripper poses (rotation + position) on each segment, scoring them by collision-free reach and contact stability. The machinery links semantics to geometry: the segmentation identifies what to grasp, while the pose generator solves how to grasp it by fitting gripper kinematics to the shape of the semantic region.

One Map to Find Them All: Real-Time Open.narr: Mobile robots navigating natural language instructions ('fetch the water bottle from the kitchen counter') must build a spatial understanding where any object can be queried by text. Traditional semantic maps are discrete, requiring separate training per object class. Building a map that supports querying by arbitrary text in real time is the challenge. This approach builds a single language-aligned feature map by fusing CLIP embeddings across camera frames into a dense 2D/3D map: every map location stores a CLIP feature, so querying for 'counter' or 'water bottle' becomes a similarity search across the map, enabling multi-object navigation without retraining.
One Map to Find Them All: Real-Time Open.how: Each camera frame is encoded into CLIP embeddings; these high-dimensional vectors are projected and fused into a dense 2D or 3D spatial grid at corresponding map coordinates (using odometry or SLAM). Every voxel or grid cell accumulates embeddings from views that observe it, either by averaging or learned fusion. To search for an object class, the query text is encoded as a CLIP embedding and compared (via cosine similarity) against all voxels in the map. The system outputs a spatial heatmap where peaks indicate locations containing the queried object, enabling navigation without retraining because the map stores raw CLIP space embeddings, not object classifiers.

Beyond Bare Queries: Open-Vocabulary Gro.narr: Language queries like 'the cup on the table' involve relationships — 'on' — and multiple objects. Grounding requires reasoning about spatial relations between objects, but open-vocabulary systems often treat each phrase as an isolated lookup. Without structured reasoning about object relationships, ambiguous or compositional phrases fail. This approach grounds queries against a 3D scene graph where nodes are detected objects and edges encode spatial relations: a query is decomposed into objects and relations, then matched to the scene graph, allowing 'the cup on the table' to be resolved by finding 'cup' nodes whose 'on' edge points to a 'table' node.
Beyond Bare Queries: Open-Vocabulary Gro.how: A 3D object detector and spatial relation classifier build a scene graph: nodes are detected object bounding boxes (labeled via CLIP or open-vocab detection), edges encode spatial relations ('on', 'in', 'behind', 'next-to') with confidence scores. A query like 'cup on table' is parsed into a subgraph template (cup-node connected via 'on' to table-node). The grounding engine matches this template against the scene graph by finding node pairs that satisfy the relations, returning all matching cup instances. The key operation is graph matching: the query decomposition turns language into a relational constraint that prunes candidates far more precisely than text-image similarity alone.

Tag Map: A Text-Based Map for Spatial Re.narr: Dense semantic maps that store VLM embeddings at every pixel are memory-intensive and slow for LLM reasoning over large spaces. Yet robots need to query maps with natural language ('where is the plant?') for navigation and planning. The bottleneck is efficiency: dense embeddings don't scale to large maps or long-horizon planning. Tag Map stores only discrete text labels (or lightweight text embeddings) at sparse landmark locations: instead of embedding every pixel, it maintains a sparse textual map where each point is tagged with descriptive text, enabling LLMs to reason over thousands of object categories at minimal memory cost.
Tag Map: A Text-Based Map for Spatial Re.how: Instead of storing CLIP embeddings (high-dimensional), the system maintains a sparse landmark map where each landmark holds only a short text descriptor ('wooden table with cups', 'red kitchen door'). As the robot explores, detected objects are converted to text captions (via MLLM or stored vocabulary) and anchored at their map locations. At query time, the LLM reads the robot's current location and nearby landmark descriptions as context, then reasons over text to answer 'what's near?' or 'navigate to where someone would prepare food'. The machinery is almost inverse to dense maps: instead of finding pixels by embedding similarity, it taps the LLM's language understanding to interpret sparse, human-readable labels, trading compute (dense embedding search) for memory (sparse text storage).

SAGE: Bridging Semantic and Actionable P.narr: A robot must understand both what a part is called ('the drawer pull') and how to manipulate it ('pull it horizontally'). These are different: semantic labels describe identity, but actionable parts require understanding motion axes and constraints specific to articulated objects. The problem is that open-vocabulary segmentation gives semantic parts, but not the motion information grasping and manipulation need. SAGE maps semantic parts to actionable affordances by learning the relationship between named parts and their degrees of freedom: for each articulated object type, it learns which semantic parts correspond to which manipulation axes, allowing 'the slider knob' to map to a linear pull affordance.
SAGE: Bridging Semantic and Actionable P.how: For each articulated object category (drawers, doors, latches), the system learns a mapping function that takes a semantic part name as input (via text embedding) and outputs a predicted affordance: a 6-DoF pose offset and a degree of freedom vector ('slide along x-axis', 'rotate around z-axis'). This is trained by collecting pairs of (part-description, motion-label) from object interactions. At test time, given 'open the slider knob', the part embedder encodes 'slider knob', the mapping function outputs the corresponding DoF (linear pull), and the robot executor applies that motion primitive to the object. The key insight is semantic grounding of affordances: language names parts, the learned model connects those names to physics, and the robot executes the inferred motion.

HERO: Hierarchical Embedding-Refinement.narr: Videos extend grounding from space to time: 'when the person picks up the mug' refers to a temporal interval, not a box. But text queries operate at multiple timescales — a moment, a clip, a scene context — and naive per-frame matching misses the hierarchical structure. The challenge is matching a linguistic event to temporal windows of varying length while maintaining cross-modal alignment. HERO constructs hierarchical embeddings at four levels (frame, clip, scene, event) and refines them with cross-modal filtering: it generates candidate temporal windows at multiple timescales, extracts multi-level features for each, then filters by similarity to the query embedding, localizing events across temporal granularities.
HERO: Hierarchical Embedding-Refinement.how: The system extracts frame-level features (per-frame CLIP embeddings), aggregates them into clip-level embeddings (short temporal windows, e.g., 2 seconds), then scene-level (entire video), and event-level (higher semantics). For each candidate temporal span, it concatenates embeddings from all four levels into a multi-scale feature vector. The refinement step applies cross-modal attention: the query embedding (text) gates which features are relevant at each temporal scale, suppressing noise at coarse levels while preserving precision at fine levels. The machinery stacks temporal aggregation followed by selective fusion: multi-timescale features + text-gated filtering localizes events by matching at the right granularity, avoiding over-smoothing from single-level embeddings.

LangField4D: Spatio-Temporal Continuous.narr: A dynamic 3D scene with moving objects requires tracking identity through time while maintaining semantic meaning. Static 3D fields store per-point features, but objects move, deform, and leave/enter the scene. Querying a dynamic scene by language ('where is the mug moving?') needs both temporal tracking and semantic alignment. LangField4D uses identity-adaptive Gaussians that group over time: it tracks moving object instances across frames using adaptive grouping, stores language-aligned features on the 4D Gaussian representation, and enables queries like 'track the blue mug' to be answered by finding the spatio-temporal region matching the description.
LangField4D: Spatio-Temporal Continuous.how: Identity-adaptive 3D Gaussians are assigned to each detected object instance and tracked across frames using temporal consistency (appearance matching + motion prediction). Each Gaussian stores a language feature vector (from CLIP) that encodes the instance's appearance and semantics. A TetraPlane or similar 4D representation fuses these Gaussian features across time, creating a continuous spatio-temporal volume where every point (x, y, z, t) has an associated language embedding. To ground 'track the blue mug', the query is encoded as a CLIP embedding, then the system traverses the 4D field finding points where the stored language feature matches the query, outputting a 3D track (one tube per frame where similarity is high). The machinery is instance tracking + feature interpolation in 4D space: identity consistency over time allows the field to maintain coherent semantics across motion.

ST4R-Splat: Spatio-Temporal Referring Se.narr: Referring segmentation in 4D requires finding the exact region a phrase points to across space and time. Standard 4D representations track geometry but not semantics; adding semantic labels per frame is expensive. The challenge is maintaining instance identity, spatial precision, and semantic meaning simultaneously in dynamic scenes. ST4R-Splat extends 4D Gaussian splatting with instance awareness and automatic MLLM captioning: it tracks object instances in the splat representation, then uses an MLLM to generate captions for each instance's motion and appearance, enabling spatial-temporal grounding by matching phrases to captioned instance tracks.
ST4R-Splat: Spatio-Temporal Referring Se.how: 4D Gaussian splatting is extended by tagging each Gaussian primitive with an instance identifier (tracking moving objects across frames). An MLLM (like LLaVA or GPT-4V) is applied to each tracked instance's rendered view, generating a caption describing its appearance and motion ('red cup sliding across table'). These captions are embedded and stored on the Gaussians. For a query like 'the object sliding left', the system encodes the query as an embedding, scans all stored captions for similarity, and marks the Gaussians of matching instances. Rendering the marked Gaussians produces a segmentation mask. The operation chain is instance tracking → auto-captioning → embedding matching → render: language grounds which objects to segment by matching generated descriptions against queries.

OmniGround: A Spatio-Temporal Grounding.narr: Evaluation of video grounding has been limited by small benchmarks with simple queries. Real-world grounding involves complex spatial relations ('to the left of'), temporal complexity ('after the person leaves'), and compositional phrases. Without a large, diverse benchmark, it's hard to drive progress on hard cases. OmniGround provides an 81-category benchmark for complex spatio-temporal grounding: it includes real-world videos with queries involving multiple objects, spatial relations, temporal constraints, and compositional descriptions, providing a standard to measure generalization to naturalistic language in dynamic scenes.
OmniGround: A Spatio-Temporal Grounding.how: The benchmark consists of 81 object categories across real videos with natural language queries that specify object identity, spatial relations ('on top of the table'), temporal constraints ('before the person sits'), and compositions ('the green mug that was moved'). Each annotation includes bounding boxes in 3D space-time (x, y, z, t, w, h, d, duration). The evaluation metric measures whether predicted 4D bounding boxes overlap with ground truth across both space and time, penalizing localization and temporal errors separately. By standardizing on real-world data with complex queries, the benchmark exposes whether models can decompose compositional language, handle occlusions, and track objects through camera motion—capabilities absent from simpler single-object or static-image benchmarks.

ReAttnCLIP: Training-Free Open-Vocabular.narr: CLIP was trained on internet photos where objects are centered and large, but remote-sensing images are overhead with tiny objects scattered across large areas. Attention patterns trained on whole-image alignment fail for small-scale detection. The problem is that CLIP's spatial attention is miscalibrated for the distribution shift from internet photos to overhead imagery. ReAttnCLIP dynamically redefinines CLIP's attention patterns for overhead imagery without retraining: it analyzes how attention should be weighted for remote-sensing image statistics, adjusting the model's focus to small objects at scale, preserving open vocabulary while adapting to domain priors.
ReAttnCLIP: Training-Free Open-Vocabular.how: CLIP's multi-head attention mechanism is analyzed to identify which query-key attention patterns dominate for standard imagery. For remote sensing (aerial overhead), small objects (cars, trees) occupy few pixels, so naive CLIP attention focuses on image-size averaging. The system computes an attention reweighting matrix that amplifies attention heads focusing on small-scale or high-frequency details, suppressing the attention patterns that average over large regions. This reweighting is applied at inference time to every CLIP forward pass without modifying weights. The machinery is adaptive attention masking: rather than retraining the model, it surgically adjusts how much each attention head contributes, making CLIP's embeddings sensitive to small objects in overhead views while preserving its open-vocabulary generality.

Exploring the Underwater World Segmentat.narr: Underwater images break CLIP: colors shift due to water absorption, scattering creates haze, and the object distribution (fish, coral, kelp) differs radically from internet photos. Off-the-shelf CLIP features perform poorly underwater. Training a new model requires labeled underwater data, which is scarce. The gap is bridging the domain without labeled data or retraining.
