This approach combines Earth2Ocean (a physics-based color-correction model) with CLIP and a large underwater dataset to establish a baseline: it corrects underwater color shifts using known water properties, then applies CLIP to the corrected images, learning to handle underwater domain shift through data-driven priors rather than retraining.
Exploring the Underwater World Segmentat.how: Underwater images suffer from color absorption: water absorbs red wavelengths more than blue, causing a color shift toward cyan. Earth2Ocean applies a physics-based color correction using estimated water depth and light wavelength absorption coefficients, reconstructing the original RGB distribution. The corrected images are then fed to standard CLIP, which outputs per-pixel embeddings. A large underwater dataset (255 categories) is used to compute class prototypes in CLIP's embedding space by averaging embeddings of all images labeled with each class. At test time, a new underwater image is color-corrected, encoded by CLIP, and segmented by assigning each pixel to the nearest class prototype. The machinery decouples domain shift (correction) from semantic embedding: physics-based preprocessing + frozen CLIP + data-driven prototypes adapts the system without retraining the vision encoder.

Thermal-Det: Language-Guided Cross-Modal.narr: Thermal images contain only heat, no RGB, yet CLIP is trained on RGB images and fails on thermal inputs. You cannot directly apply CLIP embeddings to thermal features. The solution is distillation: train a thermal backbone to mimic RGB CLIP's behavior on aligned RGB-thermal image pairs. The challenge is that CLIP operates on a fundamentally different data modality, so naive distillation may fail. Thermal-Det trains a student thermal backbone to match RGB CLIP embeddings through cross-modal distillation on paired RGB-thermal scenes: it learns a mapping from thermal features to CLIP's RGB space, enabling open-vocabulary detection on thermal images while preserving CLIP's semantic generality.
Thermal-Det: Language-Guided Cross-Modal.how: A thermal image encoder and an RGB image encoder both output feature maps for paired scenes captured simultaneously. The RGB features are passed through CLIP to produce semantic embeddings. A distillation loss trains the thermal encoder to minimize distance between its features and the RGB CLIP embeddings, learning a mapping from thermal space into CLIP's semantic space. After training, the thermal encoder can be used alone: thermal images are encoded, producing features that live in CLIP's embedding space, enabling open-vocabulary detection via similarity matching to text embeddings. The machinery is cross-modal feature alignment: the thermal encoder learns to translate its modality into a shared semantic space anchored by CLIP, avoiding the need to retrain CLIP on thermal data.

MM-OVSeg: Multimodal Optical-SAR Fusion.narr: Optical images (RGB, multispectral) and SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) images see different aspects of a scene: optical captures appearance, SAR captures physical structure and penetrates clouds. Fusing them for open-vocabulary segmentation requires finding a shared embedding space where both modalities contribute semantically. The challenge is that optical and SAR have no natural alignment and different physical meanings. MM-OVSeg fuses optical and SAR inputs by learning a joint embedding space where both modalities contribute to a unified semantic representation: it trains encoders for each modality to project into a shared CLIP-like space, then performs open-vocabulary segmentation using the fused embeddings, drawing on both view angles to ground language in multi-modal evidence.
MM-OVSeg: Multimodal Optical-SAR Fusion.how: Separate encoders process optical (RGB) and SAR (synthetic aperture radar) image patches, each outputting feature vectors. These features are projected into a shared embedding space via learned linear projections (or more complex fusion modules). The two projected features are combined (concatenation, addition, or gating) to create a fused representation. This fused feature is matched against CLIP text embeddings of semantic classes to produce per-pixel segmentation scores. Training minimizes the distance between fused features and text embeddings, jointly optimizing both encoders to agree on a common semantic space. The machinery is modality-specific encoders + learned projection + feature fusion + text matching: each modality contributes independent evidence (optical captures color, SAR penetrates clouds), and fusion combines both to ground open-vocabulary segmentation in multi-view evidence.
